bull.tldr: 21 of the sector's 32 members sit above their 50-day average and 17 of 32 posted positive 20-day returns, with four names up more than 30% over 20 sessions (MQTM +61.48%, SZTM +53.36%, CCM +41.11%, JATM +39.22%) while the median stock still trades at a P/E of just 7.29. The sector's macro_drivers list is empty (joint R² null), so this move reads as a locally-driven re-rating rather than a global-tape effect — though only 4 of 32 members carry an actual fair-value verdict, so the 'cheap' framing rests on a thin sample.
bull.case: Breadth in Textile Spinning is unusually wide for a 32-member sector: 21 names (two-thirds) trade above their 50-day SMA, and 17 of 32 closed the last 20 sessions in positive territory — this is not two or three names dragging a median. The top of that move is broad rather than a single outlier: four separate names (MQTM, SZTM, CCM, JATM) are each up more than 30% over 20 sessions, and a fifth (SERT) is up 32.21%. On the handful of names the dossier can price, valuation is inexpensive in absolute terms — median P/E 7.29, and the median fair-value gap across the 4 priced names is -8.1%. Finally, the sector carries no demonstrated global macro dependency (macro_drivers is an empty list, macro_joint_r2_pct is null), meaning today's -1.1% median session and the broader 20-day advance are being driven by sector- or name-specific capital allocation, not imported risk-off from the global tape.

bull.weakest_pillar: The 'inexpensive sector' claim (pillar 3) is built on n_valued = 4 out of 32 members — 87.5% of the sector carries no pe or fair_gap_pct at all. A median P/E of 7.29 and a -8.1% fair-value gap describe four priced names, not the sector, and cannot honestly be generalized to the other 28.

bear.tldr: The bull's valuation read leans on just 4 of 32 members carrying any fair-value verdict, and within that thin sample overvalued names (2) already outnumber undervalued ones (1). Today's session saw only 10 of 32 names advance against a median -1.1% move, the 20-day spread between MQTM's +61.48% and IDEAL's -23.03% is an 84-point gap concentrated in names with liquidity_rs_m near Rs1-2m/day, only 2 of 32 members pay any dividend at all, and the desk's own macro regime read places 'textiles/exporters' on its explicit 'avoid' list over the FY26 current-account deficit.
bear.case: The breadth argument looks weaker once the timeframe shortens: 21 of 32 names sit above their slower 50-day average, but only 10 of 32 advanced today against a median 1-day return of -1.1%, meaning better than two-thirds of the sector fell in the most recent session. Income support is essentially absent — only 2 of 32 members pay any dividend at all, with a median yield of 1.95% and median payout of just 4.11%, so there is no yield cushion to hold through the dispersion. That dispersion is extreme: the gap between the best 20-day performer (MQTM, +61.48%) and the worst (IDEAL, -23.03%) is 84 percentage points, and the largest movers on both ends trade in low single-digit Rs millions of daily liquidity (MQTM 2.2, CCM 1.2, IDEAL 1.2), which is consistent with thin-float noise rather than a fundamental sector re-rating. Layered on top of the sector's own numbers, the desk's macro read (state/macro.json) names 'textiles/exporters' explicitly on its 'avoid' tilt, citing the FY26 current-account deficit ($139mn) and unresolved Strait-of-Hormuz freight/insurance risk — a real domestic-regime headwind even though the dossier's own statistical work finds no measured global-factor beta for this sector.

bear.attacks_bull: The bull's own admitted weakest pillar — that the sector is 'inexpensive' on a median P/E of 7.29 and a -8.1% fair-value gap — fails outright on its own numbers: of the n_valued = 4 members the dossier can actually price, 2 are overvalued and only 1 is undervalued (the fourth is fair). The bull is not just working from a thin sample; the sample that exists already tilts overvalued, so 'cheap sector' is not a fair reading of even the small dataset the dossier provides.
bear.weakest_pillar: The macro-avoid pillar (pillar 4) borrows its force from state/macro.json's qualitative current-account narrative, not from this sector's own statistical work — macro_drivers here is an empty list and macro_joint_r2_pct is null, meaning no correction-survived global factor has been shown to move Textile Spinning's daily returns at all. The current-account/exporter linkage is a plausible fundamental channel, but the dossier itself has not measured it as a demonstrated relationship on this sector's price action.

bull_rebuttal: The bear's valuation attack is conceded in substance: with 2 of the 4 priced members verdicted overvalued and only 1 undervalued, 'the sector is cheap' overreaches what n_valued = 4 of 32 can support, and the bull narrows the claim accordingly — the honest statement is that a handful of larger, model-covered names (SHDT undervalued at fair_gap_pct +85.7%, KOHTM and TATM overvalued) trade cheap on an absolute P/E basis, not that the 32-name sector as a whole is undervalued. On the macro-avoid attack, the bull holds its ground: state/macro.json's 'avoid' tilt for textiles/exporters is a judgment about exposure to the current-account channel, and the dossier's own correction-survived macro_drivers analysis finds no demonstrated daily-return relationship (empty list, null R²) — the two claims operate on different evidence tiers, and conflating a qualitative regime worry with a measured beta would be the actual error here.

house_view.tldr: The desk's read leans cautious: today's session saw only 10 of 32 members advance (median -1.1%) after a 20-day advance built on names paying almost no dividend (2 of 32 payers) and priced almost nowhere (4 of 32 with a fair-value verdict, and that small sample already tilts overvalued 2-to-1), while the desk's own macro regime names textiles/exporters an explicit avoid over the FY26 current-account deficit. Conviction stays low because the sector carries zero demonstrated global-factor beta (macro_drivers empty, joint R² null) and the 21-of-32-above-50-day breadth genuinely has not broken yet — one down session does not settle the debate either way.
house_view.summary: The evidence supports tempering the bull's breadth story rather than adopting it outright. Two-thirds of the sector sits above its 50-day average and 17 of 32 posted positive 20-day returns, which is real and broad — but the valuation leg of the bull case collapses on its own numbers (2 of 4 priced members overvalued, 1 undervalued) and the income leg barely exists (2 of 32 payers, 1.95% median yield), leaving nothing to anchor conviction if the momentum leg fades. Today's session is itself a soft warning: only 10 of 32 names advanced against a median -1.1% move, and the 84-point gap between the sector's best and worst 20-day performers is concentrated in names trading in low single-digit Rs millions of daily liquidity — a pattern more consistent with thin-float speculative flow than a durable re-rating. Layered on top, the desk's macro regime read is explicitly risk-off and names 'textiles/exporters' as an avoid over the FY26 current-account deficit ($139mn) and unresolved Strait-of-Hormuz freight/insurance risk. That domestic-regime concern is a fundamental judgment, not a statistically measured beta on this sector's own price series (macro_drivers is empty here, joint R² is null), so it is weighted as a headwind on the sector's earnings/export channel rather than as evidence the sector trades with global risk sentiment day to day.

house_view.dissent: The strongest case against this cautious stance is the bull's breadth argument, and it survives the bear's attack largely intact. Twenty-one of 32 members — two-thirds of a 32-name sector — trade above their 50-day average, and 17 of 32 posted a positive 20-day return; that is a genuinely broad base, not two or three speculative names dragging a median, and four separate names (MQTM, SZTM, CCM, JATM) plus a fifth (SERT) are each up more than 30% over 20 sessions. The bear's rebuttal to this leans entirely on a single session (10 of 32 advancing, median -1.1%), and one down day does not erase a 20-day base; if today's print is noise rather than the start of a reversal, breadth could hold or extend through the sector's two nearest catalysts, GADT's results on 2026-08-04 and TATM's on 2026-08-06. Just as importantly, the macro-avoid argument this house view leans on is explicitly not a measured relationship: macro_drivers for Textile Spinning is an empty list and macro_joint_r2_pct is null, meaning no correction-survived statistical work ties this sector's actual daily returns to any global factor, let alone to the current-account narrative in macro.json. That narrative is a plausible fundamental channel (exporters facing a weaker external account and unresolved freight risk), but it is a qualitative overlay applied from outside this sector's own price data, not a demonstrated beta — a reader who weights the dossier's own statistical findings over the macro desk's qualitative judgment would reasonably conclude this house view is importing a headwind the sector's own numbers have not yet shown.

claims.text: Textile Spinning's median member return underperforms the KSE-100 over the 20 trading sessions following 2026-08-01, as thin income support (2 of 32 payers, 1.95% median yield) and today's narrow one-day breadth (10 of 32 advancing, median -1.1%) fail to sustain the prior 20-day advance (median +1.35%) against the desk's domestic risk-off regime and its explicit textiles/exporters avoid tilt.

The 20-day return spread between Textile Spinning's best and worst performers (currently MQTM +61.48% vs IDEAL -23.03%, an 84-percentage-point gap concentrated in names trading below Rs3m/day liquidity) narrows to under 40 percentage points by 2026-08-31, consistent with the current dispersion being thin-float noise rather than a durable sector-wide re-rating.
